title: Question about Art generation and path to take
author: Humble_Operation_501
selftext:
Hi, I'm really interested in developing a survival RPG game and I was able to generate the exact art style i want and Id like to implement it 1:1 with the exact art style. 2 questions

1. Whats the art style called? I cant find anything like it
2. If I wanna start with implementation through AI to generate Characters and Environment what option should I go with? Claude, Codex? and is there a guide on how to start with Art in AI? Thank you!

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: Claude doesn't do images. Codex is for coding. For making images use chat gpt or googles nano banana. Just feed the AI the image and have them describe a prompt for it.

replies.author: Humble_Operation_501
replies.body: Thanks! I read about a few specific AI 3D generation tools like meshy.ai - how do they do in comparison? Worth looking into?

replies.author: Kingnorik
replies.body: Making 3D is hard. Even with AI, even with 3D meshes from meshy. I've used meshy very extensivevly. It produces good looking stuff. The challenge is getting that stuff to animate and look good while not destroying your target audiences computer.

replies.author: samuele_v
replies.body:
I wouldn't say it's "impossible", but yes, nailing down that exact style is going to be tough. Buildings, lamp-posts, rocks, fences are all pretty much doable in Meshy and would more or less come out the way they are in the pictures (with the exception of those on the horizon which will be trickier to handle). Terrain seems to be more on the painterly side than realistic with the exception of cobblestone, so that can be a mix of flat primitives and some free textures. Lamps can work by adding flame VFXs inside of them manually. Toughest part is probably going to be the general lighting/mood and, of course, animating the character in a credible way. Not to mention the patience to add all those elements manually in the map (what AI severely lacks today in my opinion is spatial awareness).

This is all out of my head from my experience with Godot - I wouldn't know about Unity and UE.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
They are a couple years away from being production ready for games in one gen. Some studios claim to be using fine-tuned versions that CAN generate production ready assets for very specific purposes, and have worked with companies like Meshy to facilitate that. For us indies that is not an option, to my knowledge. So if you want to use it in a game, you're going to need to know how to model, texture and animate already, that way you have the skills required to fix up the model it spits out.  The models look great but do a very poor job when it comes to keeping poly count at acceptable levels, and will generally end up with severe animation issues and/or poor texture bakes as a result. There are a lot of guides out there on how to fix the models up, but it is not easy and even once you know what you are doing it is one or more hours of work, not counting rigging (and if it's not a humanoid then animation libraries are limited and you're going to be hand animating.) 

That's not to say it's impossible or that they can't still save you time (modeling a detailed 3d sculpt could take half a day on its own depending on the detail level, and this really cuts into that time since you can just sculpt a low poly version and bake the meshy output onto it.) But there's a reason you don't see indies trying to push out Diablo 4 level graphics, or at least not via AI genned assets. You're better off with asset packs / store bought assets generally, from a time perspective, if you're a one man team with no dedicated artist.

Alternatively build the game in a simpler style. Can always upgrade the graphics to the style you want later if you plan for that possibility, once the gameplay itself is working.

replies.author: Mecradore
replies.body:
Use Meshy only for concepts or distance objects the player can't reach. It makes things faster but it definitely isn't the best quality. I tried some of the major ai modeling tools and Meshy was the best. It's great at overall thick concepts but fails at fine detail if your expecting to only give 1 image. You'll probably get better results if you use composition images, and then remesh for lower poly.

I haven't experimented much but you're probably better off with that composition image and an MCP server to blender or your favorite modeling program.

Good luck out there!! Keep us posted, **LOVE** the art style!!

comments.author: hblok
comments.body:
Feed the image into gpt and ask it to give an analysis or prompt with exact details regarding style, mood, colors, composition, etc, etc. If there's a detail it missed, ask again.

That should hopefully give you a good base to generate further images which look similar.

The challenge is of course if you now want different perspective and composition. At that point, I'd probably try to split up the notes, and connect gpt to a git repo to read from.

comments.author: CautiousCarry4209
comments.body: It is not easy and very time consuming to recreate that picture in 3D. I recommend to use isometric view with a mix of tiles, images and sprites. That is probably the easiest path to the style you are going for.

comments.author: Bewbsnballs
comments.body: You’re not making this with AI right now, however those are just stylized assets (like modern Fortnite style, so leaning more realism than toon) paired with nice lighting, post processing, and fog/fire vfx. All things you can find affordably in asset packs.

comments.author: Hahnter
comments.body:
I’ve been messing around with game development using AI. I told myself I was going to avoid generating artwork and designs when I can, so I’ve been using AI strictly for coding and implementing pre-made assets instead. I I’ve also been considering using my photography to generate textures and 3D models demon Meshy. 

I’d say the easiest way to get your game to look like that is to use pre-made assets that are already available and then just mess with the lighting.
